  collapse = TRUE,
  comment = "#>"

The [pdftools](https://docs.ropensci.org/pdftools/) package is available for importing PDF files. However, this package does not work optimally when importing PDF files with multiple columns and text boxes. Since the `pdftools::pdf_text()` function from the `pdftools` package processes text line by line, it often fails to maintain the context of the text. As a result, the output may contain sentences with unrelated fragments of text from different parts of the page. Words that are not placed in the correct context are unsuitable for text analysis.

However, the words grouped into clusters by this package using a Density-Based Spatial Clustering algorithm are likely to be contextually related and thus suitable for text analysis. This package directly utilizes the clustering algorithms implemented in the [dbscan](https://github.com/mhahsler/dbscan) package.

## Loading Packages

```{r setup}
library(pdftextclusteR)
```

## Example Data

The examples in this vignette use the `cibap` dataset that is bundled with the package: the report *Kwaliteitsagenda 2024-2027 Cibap*, published on [rijksoverheid.nl](https://www.rijksoverheid.nl/documenten/rapporten/2024/09/16/kwaliteitsagenda-2024-2027-cibap). This document was chosen because it contains several pages with columns, text boxes and different layouts. The package also bundles a second, similar dataset: `npo`.

Both datasets are `PdfDocument` objects, created by reading the PDF file with `pdf_read()`. To apply the same workflow to your own documents, read them the same way (or simply pass the path directly to `pdf_detect_clusters()`):

```{r, eval = FALSE}
my_document <- pdf_read("path/to/document.pdf")
```

A `PdfDocument` contains one `PdfPage` per page: a tibble of words with their position, size and font, plus the page number and page dimensions. Pages are accessed with `[[`, subsets with `[`:

```{r}
cibap
cibap[[18]]
```

The underlying word data of a page (or a whole document) is available via `as_tibble()`:

```{r}
head(tibble::as_tibble(cibap[[18]]), 5)
```

## Inspecting the objects

All three object types have a compact `print()` and a `summary()` method. For a document, `summary()` returns a tibble with the number of words (and, once clustered, clusters) per page — convenient for spotting problem pages:

```{r}
overview <- summary(cibap)
head(overview, 3)
```

For a single page, `summary()` shows which fonts are used — a quick way to understand the structure of a page:

```{r}
summary(cibap[[18]])
```

Object properties are accessed with `@`:

```{r}
cibap[[18]]@number
cibap[[18]]@width
```

## Detecting text clusters

### Single page clustering

Clusters - usually columns and text boxes - are detected with the `pdf_detect_clusters()` function. When applied to a single page, the function returns a tibble with each word assigned to a cluster.

```{r}
cibap_clusters <- cibap[[18]] |>
  pdf_detect_clusters()

cibap_clusters
```

The result is a `PdfClusters` object: the same page, with each word assigned to a cluster (column `.cluster`; cluster 0 is noise):

```{r}
head(tibble::as_tibble(cibap_clusters), 5)
```

### Multiple page clustering

One of the key features of `pdftextclusteR` is the ability to process multiple pages at once. This is particularly useful when analyzing entire documents. Let's process the first 10 pages of the example document:

```{r}
multiple_page_clusters <- cibap[1:10] |>
  pdf_detect_clusters()

multiple_page_clusters
```

The result is a `PdfDocument` whose pages now are `PdfClusters` objects. The function automatically displays a progress bar when processing multiple pages and provides a summary of the results.

Progress bars and messages can be suppressed with the `verbose` argument, or globally with `options(pdftextclusteR.verbose = FALSE)`:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
cibap[1:10] |>
  pdf_detect_clusters(verbose = FALSE)
```

## Plotting the Clusters

### Plotting a single page

Using the `pdf_plot_clusters()` function, you can create a visual representation of the detected clusters for a single page:

```{r pdf_plot_clusters, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 5}
cibap_clusters |>
  pdf_plot_clusters()
```

`plot()` and `ggplot2::autoplot()` are available as aliases: `plot(cibap_clusters)` gives the same result.

The cluster numbers indicate the reading order: the order in which `pdf_extract_clusters()` will return the text. Use `show_order = TRUE` to draw arrows between the clusters and verify that order at a glance:

```{r, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 5}
cibap_clusters |>
  pdf_plot_clusters(show_order = TRUE)
```

For a clustered page, `summary()` gives a per-cluster overview with a text preview:

```{r}
summary(cibap_clusters)
```

If you compare this with the original PDF page, you can see that the package has clustered the text quite accurately in this case:

![Page 18 of the original cibap report](images/example_pdf.png)

### Plotting multiple pages

The `pdf_plot_clusters()` function can also be applied to multiple pages:

```{r, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 5}
# Plot the tenth page of the multiple page result
multiple_page_clusters[[10]] |>
  pdf_plot_clusters()
```

You can plot all pages at once, which returns a list of ggplot objects:

```{r, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 5}
# This returns a list of ggplot objects
all_plots <- multiple_page_clusters |>
  pdf_plot_clusters()

# You can access individual plots
all_plots[[8]]
```

## Extract text from clusters

### Extracting from a single page

The text of the detected clusters can be extracted with the `pdf_extract_clusters()` function:

```{r}
cibap_clusters_text <- cibap_clusters |>
  pdf_extract_clusters()

# View the first 5 clusters
head(cibap_clusters_text, 5)
```

Words that could not be assigned to any cluster (noise) are excluded from the extraction by default. Use `include_noise = TRUE` to include them as cluster 0.

### Filtering out chart and figure text

Note the bottom-right area of the example page: it contains a map and a bar chart. The words there are chart labels — category names, numbers, axis labels. The clustering is purely geometric, so labels that happen to sit close together are grouped into clusters, but these fragments are not running text and are usually meaningless for text analysis.

Such fragments are easy to recognize in the output: they form clusters with very few words. The `word_count` column can be used to filter them out:

```{r}
cibap_clusters_text |>
  dplyr::filter(word_count >= 10)
```

The threshold depends on your document; `pdf_plot_clusters()` is a convenient way to check which clusters you are keeping.

### Extracting from multiple pages

When extracting from multiple pages, the function returns a single tibble with an extra `page` column containing the real page numbers:

```{r}
multiple_page_text <- multiple_page_clusters |>
  pdf_extract_clusters()

multiple_page_text |>
  dplyr::filter(page == 5) |>
  head(5)
```

If you prefer a list with a separate tibble for each page, use `combine = FALSE`:

```{r}
multiple_page_text_list <- multiple_page_clusters |>
  pdf_extract_clusters(combine = FALSE)

# View the first 5 clusters from the fifth page
head(multiple_page_text_list[[5]], 5)
```

## Classifying text types

Not every cluster is running text: pages contain headings, page headers and footers, page numbers and chart labels. `pdf_classify_clusters()` assigns a type to every cluster. It works on document level, because the strongest signals span pages: headers and footers repeat in the same position, and page numbers increase in step with the page index.

```{r}
classified <- cibap |>
  pdf_detect_clusters(verbose = FALSE) |>
  pdf_classify_clusters()
```

The types are visible in the plot with `color_by = ".type"`:

```{r, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 5}
classified[[18]] |>
  pdf_plot_clusters(color_by = ".type")
```

Classification also improves the reading order: page furniture (headers, footers, page numbers) is moved to the end of the cluster order, out of the reading flow.

After classification, the extraction gains `.type` and `.type_level` columns, and unwanted types can be excluded:

```{r}
classified[[18]] |>
  pdf_extract_clusters(exclude = c("page_footer", "figure_text")) |>
  head(5)
```

The thresholds are bundled in a rules object that can be tuned. See the article [Text types and reading order](https://coeneisma.github.io/pdftextclusteR/articles/text-types.html) for how the classification works, how it interacts with the reading order, and how to tune it.

## The one-step pipeline

For the common case — clean text, no page furniture — `pdf_extract_text()` runs the whole pipeline (read, detect, classify, order, extract) with sensible defaults:

```{r}
cibap[15:20] |>
  pdf_extract_text(verbose = FALSE) |>
  head(5)
```

It also accepts a file path directly: `pdf_extract_text("path/to/document.pdf")`.

## Different algorithms

The [dbscan](https://github.com/mhahsler/dbscan) package is used to detect the clusters. This package supports four different algorithms:

-   `dbscan`: The default algorithm, which generally provides good results

-   `jpclust`: Jarvis-Patrick clustering algorithm

-   `sNNclust`: Shared nearest neighbor clustering

-   `hdbscan`: Hierarchical DBSCAN

Each algorithm has different parameters that can be tuned for optimal results:

```{r, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 5}
# Example with sNNclust algorithm
cibap[[18]] |>
  pdf_detect_clusters(algorithm = "sNNclust", k = 5, eps = 2, minPts = 3) |>
  pdf_plot_clusters()
```

```{r, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 5}
# Example with hdbscan algorithm
cibap[[18]] |>
  pdf_detect_clusters(algorithm = "hdbscan", minPts = 2) |>
  pdf_plot_clusters()
```

## Complete workflow example

Here's a complete workflow example that processes multiple pages, plots the results, and extracts the text:

```{r, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 5}
# Select pages 5-7
selected_pages <- cibap[5:7]

# Detect clusters across all pages
clusters <- selected_pages |>
  pdf_detect_clusters()

# Plot clusters for visualization (just showing the first page plot)
plots <- clusters |>
  pdf_plot_clusters()
plots[[1]]
```

```{r}
# Extract text from all clusters
text_data <- clusters |>
  pdf_extract_clusters()

# The largest clusters in the selection
text_data |>
  dplyr::arrange(dplyr::desc(word_count)) |>
  head(3)
```

## Conclusion

The `pdftextclusteR` package provides a robust solution for extracting text from PDFs with complex layouts, such as multiple columns and text boxes. By using density-based spatial clustering algorithms, it can accurately identify text blocks that belong together, making it suitable for various text analysis tasks.

Key features:

-   Support for multiple clustering algorithms

-   Processing of single pages or entire documents

-   Visualization of detected clusters

-   Extraction of text from clusters with word count statistics

-   Progress tracking for multi-page documents

For more details on specific functions and parameters, refer to the package documentation.
